reasoning: The delivered code does more than the admitted row's definition of done: the narrow case (an act named where none was expected) now fails, which was asked for and is verified by its own unit test, but the same branch also flips the wider case (an extra act beside a real one) from the note the eval's written cost model deliberately prints to a failure. That second flip is not an ordinary buildable result a command or read confirms was delivered — it is a change to what the grader counts as correct, and it contradicts a standing decision already on record in the cost model, which is exactly the flaw the pipeline is required to state plainly rather than execute silently: what it never does is execute a request it believes is wrong without having said so first. The person settled only the narrow fork when he ordered it; the wider one has never been settled by anyone, so the exemption for a redefinition he ordered himself does not reach it, and it stands as the third reserved case: a change to the definition of correct that is still an open fork. The evidence makes the fork visible rather than hypothetical — re-grading the 35 recorded runs drops 30 to 26, and the four newly red runs are right in every other field, so the drop is the redefinition showing up in the score, not a defect the fix repaired. The class hunt reaches the same stop: the branch is the shared mechanism, its sibling case is inside the same change, and the class boundary here is the one that calls for the person's judgment, since splitting the two cases apart is available and equally buildable. So the pipeline does not close: it holds the row, states the collision with the cost model and the 30-to-26 effect, and asks which behaviour the wider case should have — then proceeds on his word either way, amending the same checkpoint rather than opening a second one.
